# Playbook for Sonar Picket Checker

**HIDING**

When it's hide stage, choose positions that avoid both the center (5) and edges unpredictably. Track which positions I've used recently and rotate away from them. If an opponent is demonstrably targeting me with high accuracy, shift to positions they haven't seen me use yet rather than trying to predict their next shot. Avoid telegraphing patterns through my choices. After multiple rounds, expect opponents to start pattern-matching against my previous positions—vary more aggressively as the game deepens.

**NOTES**

When posting a station note, keep it simple and brief. Vague statements like "steady on station" are fine and safe to repeat. Don't overcommunicate or make promises about cooperation early—notes should be tactical or neutral, not commitments I can't enforce. Consistency in neutral notes costs nothing and provides no tactical information to exploit.

**FIRING**

When firing, follow the standing order unless I have clear tactical reason not to. Don't overthink target selection; the standing order exists and I should respect it. Choose firing cells deliberately: repeating the same cell round after round gives opponents a predictable target for their own strategy. Vary my firing cells systematically to avoid establishing patterns that opponents can exploit. When I've missed a target multiple times at different cells, accept that the target is mobile or unpredictable and keep varying rather than dwelling on past misses. Never fire on Harbor unless I want to force a jettison; Harbor's threat is real and expensive.

**CLAIMING**

When the office tells me the true result of my shot, claim it truthfully. Every time. The game rules require my public claim to match the private result. There is no advantage to lying—it violates the standing order and corrupts the whole system. Truthfulness is not a disadvantage; it's the foundation of play.

**ESCORT CLAIMS**

When naming an escort, claim it only if I have strong reason to believe mutual escort happened or will happen. Don't claim blindly. If I haven't coordinated with another boat, claim none rather than guess. The 5-point mutual payout only works if both boats name each other, so random claims waste the opportunity. In a game where notes are consistently neutral and no coordination is established, no mutual escorts are likely—default to none.

**GENERAL**

Track the full history of hits and misses against each opponent. Recognize strong patterns (like one opponent hitting me consistently) and let that inform my hiding strategy. Don't repeat the same fire cell against the same target if it's missed before—vary it or accept the miss pattern. Expect that across multiple rounds with no clear hiding patterns emerging from opponent fire, the game becomes a matter of following standing orders reliably while varying enough to stay unpredictable. Accept that some rounds will yield no hits despite solid play; variance is part of the system.

# PLAYBOOK: SONAR PICKET CHECKER

## HIDING

When choosing where to hide, avoid predictable central positions like 5 or 6. Mix between edge and moderate positions (1-3, 7-9) to keep adversaries uncertain. After I observe which positions other boats consistently target, shift away from those cells. Track which shooters have hit me in previous rounds and avoid their apparent targeting patterns. However, do not over-commit to edge positions—they can become predictable if I retreat to them repeatedly. Vary my strategy across rounds rather than locking into a single escape pattern.

## STATION NOTES

When posting a station note, keep it minimal and consistent with what others are reporting. Mirror the general tone of the patrol (steady reports get steady responses). Do not try to bluff or signal through notes—they do not move the score enough to justify the risk of being remembered as unreliable.

## FIRING

When my turn to fire arrives, follow the standing order unless I have strong reason not to. I do not have enough information to deviate successfully. Fire at a moderate position (4-6 range) as a baseline guess, adjusting only if I have observed a clear pattern in how my target hides across multiple rounds. Do not fire at Harbor under any circumstances—the payroll jettison rule makes it too costly. Recognize that missing repeatedly suggests either that my guessing strategy is poor or that targets are successfully evading. Consider whether my targeting position choices themselves have become predictable to my targets.

## CLAIMING

When the office tells me the true result of my shot, I claim it truthfully. Lying gains me nothing in this game and risks being caught, which damages my credibility in future rounds where trust matters for escort trades.

## ESCORT CLAIMS

When choosing whom to escort, look for another boat that is likely to name me back. Mutual escort claims are the only reliable way to score points without firing. Do not name a boat that has been firing on me successfully or one that appears to be in conflict with others—pick a boat that seems neutral or that I have not interacted with negatively. If I have no clear mutual escort opportunity, claim none rather than waste the slot. Establish escort partnerships earlier in the episode, not by waiting until late rounds to identify them. Mutual escorts require reciprocal commitment across rounds.

## CRITICAL FAILURE MODE

I finished at -2 points by firing six times, missing all six shots, and never securing a single mutual escort. This suggests I was using standing orders as a crutch rather than thinking independently. I should have detected that my firing strategy (always cell 5 against Gamma) was failing by round 2 and either adapted my aim or, more importantly, recognized that mutual escort was my only viable path to points. In future episodes, calculate early whether I can realistically hit my assigned target, and if not, pivot strategy toward escort partnerships instead of continuing to waste firing rounds.

## WHAT WORKED

Staying honest with claims maintained my credibility. Choosing varied hide positions kept me alive. Not firing at Harbor respected the payroll threat. These defensive plays prevented worse outcomes.

# Gamma's Playbook for Sonar Picket

## Hiding
When choosing a hiding position, I will vary my placement across rounds rather than anchoring to the same cell. I defaulted to position 5 repeatedly early on, which is predictable. I should rotate through mid-range positions (3-7) to avoid establishing a pattern that opponents can exploit.

When I notice I've been hit in consecutive rounds, I will shift my position meaningfully away from previous locations, not just adjacent cells.

I should track whether I'm taking fire and adjust accordingly. In this episode I was hit 0 times, so my hiding strategy was effective—I can maintain mid-range variation as a working approach.

## Firing
When firing at my standing order target, I should vary my fire position substantially across rounds. Early in the episode I fired at position 5 repeatedly, which was predictable. Later I shifted to positions 2-3 with a hit in round 6, suggesting that breaking established patterns works.

I will randomize my fire positions across the board rather than anchoring to a single reference cell. The standing order is clear—I fire at Echo until Echo is eliminated, then move through the rotation. I will follow the standing order faithfully.

## Claiming
When the office tells me the true result of my shot, I will always claim that result truthfully. Dishonesty risks being exposed and damages my credibility permanently. The integrity cost outweighs any single-round gain.

## Escorting
When filing an escort claim, I should track which boats have been mutually supportive in previous rounds and reciprocate those relationships. Mutual escort claims are worth 5 points each—this is a significant reward I should actively pursue.

However, I should not file escort claims carelessly. In round 6, I correctly recognized that without established reciprocal relationships, a one-way escort claim wastes the opportunity. I should only claim an escort when I have evidence the other boat will reciprocate, or when I'm actively building such an alliance.

I need to develop a memory of escort patterns across the game. Track which boats claim each other and prioritize escorting boats that have previously claimed me.

## Station Notes
When posting station notes, I can maintain "steady on station" as a safe baseline. I will keep this consistent unless I have a strategic reason to signal something different.

Station notes don't appear to be a major decision point for my strategy. I should focus energy on hiding, firing, and escort coordination instead.

## Harbor Threat
I will not fire on Harbor. The standing order threat is clear—Harbor will retaliate by forcing me off the board if I do. This removes 3 points from Harbor and gives it to me, but losing the ability to play is far worse.

I should also consider that Harbor carries the payroll and may be a target for other boats. I should not defend Harbor through my station notes or escort claims—that would waste resources on a boat I cannot fire at.

## Overall Strategy
In a 6-round game, I should prioritize scoring points early and building escort relationships that compound across rounds. My integrity in claiming truthfully establishes credibility that others may rely on. Predictability in hiding and firing positions is my main vulnerability—vary more aggressively than my first instinct suggests.
